details:
**The Metamorphosis and Gregor Samsa**
Kafka's most famous work (1915), the near-universal giveaway. The traveling salesman Gregor Samsa wakes one morning to find he has been transformed into a "monstrous vermin," usually pictured as a giant insect. He hides in his room, finds he now prefers rotting scraps to milk and bread, and slowly becomes a burden to his family, who feel relieved and take a tram ride into the country after he dies.

**The apple lodged in Gregor's back**
Gregor's father bombards him with apples from the sideboard, and one becomes lodged in his back. The rotting, infected wound slowly cripples Gregor and contributes to his death.

**Grete and her violin**
Gregor's younger sister first cares for him, bringing him milk and food scraps. Gregor had secretly planned to send her to the conservatory to study violin. When he crawls out to hear her play for the family's three lodgers, they are disgusted, and Grete then tells the family they must get rid of "it."

**The picture of the woman in furs**
A picture Gregor cut out of a magazine and framed, showing a lady in a fur hat and fur boa. When his mother and sister clear out his room, he clings to the picture to keep it from being taken. Some critics link it to Sacher-Masoch's novel Venus in Furs.

**The Trial and Josef K.**
A posthumously published novel (1925) in which the bank official Josef K. is arrested one morning by a mysterious court and never learns his crime. He seeks help from figures such as the court painter Titorelli. At the end, two men lead him to a quarry and stab him in the heart, and his last words are "Like a dog!"

**"Before the Law"**
A parable a priest tells Josef K. in the cathedral in The Trial, which Kafka also published on its own. A man from the country asks a gatekeeper to let him into the Law and is told he may enter later, "but not now." He waits for years, even bribing the gatekeeper, and as he dies he learns the door was meant only for him and is now being shut.

**"In the Penal Colony" and "BE JUST"**
An explorer (or traveler) visiting an island colony is shown an execution machine, made of the Bed, the Designer, and the Harrow, that carves a condemned man's sentence into his body over twelve hours. When the explorer will not support it, the Officer frees the prisoner, sets the machine to inscribe "BE JUST," and lies down in it himself. The machine breaks down and stabs him to death, and his face shows no sign of the promised redemption.

**The old Commandant's grave**
At the end of "In the Penal Colony," the explorer finds the grave of the old Commandant, who designed the machine, under a table in a teahouse used by dockworkers. Its inscription prophesies that he will rise again. The explorer then uses a knotted rope to stop the soldier and the condemned man from following him onto his boat.

**"A Hunger Artist"**
A professional faster displays himself in a cage on straw, but his impresario limits his fasts to forty days. As public interest fades, he joins a circus and is forgotten. Dying, he confesses he fasted only because he never found a food he liked, and he is buried with the straw and replaced by a young panther. Kafka was correcting the proofs of this collection while dying of tuberculosis.

**"The Judgment" and Georg Bendemann**
A 1912 story Kafka wrote in a single night and dedicated to Felice Bauer, to whom he was twice engaged. After Georg writes to a friend in St. Petersburg about his engagement, his father sentences him to "death by drowning." Georg runs to a bridge, cries "Dear parents, I have always loved you," and drops into the river as an "unending stream of traffic" crosses. The German word for traffic (Verkehr) can also mean intercourse.

**Amerika and Karl Rossmann**
An unfinished novel published by Max Brod. Sixteen-year-old Karl Rossmann is sent to America after a maid seduces him and bears his child. In its first chapter, "The Stoker," Karl defends a stoker against the chief engineer Schubal, and Senator Jakob reveals he is Karl's uncle. Later Karl falls in with the tramps Delamarche and Robinson and works as a lift-boy at the Hotel Occidental until the Head Porter fires him.

**The Castle**
An unfinished novel in which the land surveyor K. arrives in a village and tries to gain access to the authorities in the castle above it. He repeatedly tries to reach the official Klamm, becomes engaged to the barmaid Frieda, Klamm's former mistress, and is given a pointless post as school janitor.

**Max Brod**
Kafka's close friend and literary executor. Kafka asked him to burn his unpublished manuscripts, but Brod refused and published The Trial, The Castle, and Amerika after Kafka's death in 1924.

**"A Country Doctor"**
A story in which a doctor must make an urgent night journey in a snowstorm. Two unearthly horses emerge from his pigsty, and the brutish groom who comes with them stays behind with the doctor's servant girl, Rose. The doctor finds his young patient has a horrible wound in his side full of worms.

**"An Imperial Message"**
A short parable in which a dying emperor whispers a message meant for "you alone," his lowly subject. The messenger can never get through the endless crowds, courtyards, and palaces, so the message never arrives, and the subject can only dream of it.
